paper_metadata.title: Quantum advantage of Monte Carlo option pricing

summary: This paper studies quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo option pricing for European call options using quantum amplitude estimation, comparing rescaling and Fourier-series payoff approximations under depolarizing noise in Qiskit simulations. The authors report that quantum advantage would require CX error rates around 10^-6 to 10^-7, with about 20 logical qubits potentially sufficient, while current IBM CX errors are about 10^-2 to 10^-3; the Fourier method consistently outperforms rescaling and reduces the systematic-to-statistical error ratio from about 0.7 to about 0.1.

experiments.description: Quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo option pricing for European call options using amplitude estimation, comparing rescaling and Fourier-series function approximation under depolarizing noise in Qiskit simulations.

algorithm.variant: Quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC) with standard Quantum Amplitude Estimation; compared rescaling vs Fourier-series payoff approximation
algorithm.optimizer: maximum likelihood estimation for amplitude estimation; no variational optimizer

hyperparameters.grover_schedule: exponentially increasing schedule with base 2; m0=0, mk=2^(k-1) for k>0
hyperparameters.shots_per_grover_step: Nshot=100 in many simulations; varied to satisfy error threshold

problem_formulation.encoding_details: The discretized log-normal stock-price distribution is loaded into amplitudes of an n-qubit state; a comparator marks payoff qubit when Si > K; payoff is approximated either by rescaling or Fourier-series construction.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate the discounted expected payoff of a European call option: E[e^{-rT} max(ST-K,0)]
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Comparator circuit for payoff thresholding; truncation and discretization of the probability distribution; systematic-error control via parameter optimization
problem_formulation.num_ancilla_qubits: n ancilla qubits for comparator; additional payoff qubit

problem_instance.description: European call option pricing under the Black-Scholes-Merton model with log-normal underlying distribution.

dataset_specification.description: At-the-money options with S0=K=2, T=1, r in {0.05,0.1,0.2}, nu in {0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4}

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Truncate the log-normal distribution to a finite interval controlled by w; discretize into 2^n bins; exact state preparation used for the discretized distribution
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Noisy and exact Qiskit simulations; parameter grid search over n, w, c, lmax, and Grover schedule; results averaged over 11 options in some plots; maximum-likelihood simulations repeated 1000 times for a simple 2-qubit case to estimate standard deviation

noise_model.noise_type: depolarizing channel on 1-qubit and 2-qubit gates; effective Grover-operator coherence probability fit from gate-level noise

implementation_details.transpilation_target: IBM native basis gates {CX, X, SX, RZ}
implementation_details.classical_solver: maximum likelihood estimation; classical Black-Scholes closed-form benchmark
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Closed-form Black-Scholes variance and option price used for classical benchmark; parameter sweeps over option and algorithm settings
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Quantum advantage metric Q computed from ratio of classical and quantum errors; systematic and statistical errors combined in quadrature

speedup_claims.conditions: assuming ideal quantum amplitude estimation and ignoring hardware noise/systematic errors
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper emphasizes that systematic errors and depolarizing noise can eliminate practical advantage on current hardware.

speedup_claims.factor: around 1e-6 to 1e-7 CX error rate required for advantage
speedup_claims.conditions: European call option pricing with optimized QAMC under depolarizing noise
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a threshold estimate from simulations, not a hardware demonstration.

speedup_claims.factor: about 20 logical qubits may be sufficient
speedup_claims.conditions: for quantum advantage in the studied option-pricing setup
speedup_claims.caveats: This is an estimate from numerical optimization, not an experimentally verified requirement.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/N) estimation error for QAE; quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(1/sqrt(N)) estimation error for classical Monte Carlo; Monte Carlo convergence as baseline
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Paper estimates quantum advantage may appear around ~20 logical qubits and at CX error rates around 1e-6 to 1e-7

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: ~20 logical qubits; CX error rate around 10^-6 to 10^-7
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: About 20 logical qubits, low-noise two-qubit gates, and error-corrected or near-error-corrected hardware; the paper’s own simulations only reach 13 state-preparation qubits (27 total qubits) in noisy simulation
limiting_factors: Strong systematic errors from state preparation and function approximation
Current IBM CX errors around 10^-2 to 10^-3

notes: circuit_depth is not given as a single depth number; inferred only qualitatively from Grover schedule length and maximum iterations.
num_qubits 2n+1 is explicitly stated; the 27-qubit figure is inferred from n=13 simulation limit.
Hardware is a noisy simulator in Qiskit; no real QPU experiment is reported.

The paper claims quantum advantage is possible in principle for European option pricing, but only under very low CX error rates and with about 20 logical qubits; the evidence is from noisy simulation, not a QPU demonstration.
